claims.text: A hybrid approach combining first-principles molecular dynamics and machine-learned interatomic potentials will predict electronic conductivity in bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than perfect-crystal analytical models over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen is single phase.
Approximately 1 wt.% oxygen introduces point defects and local lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
First-principles molecular dynamics can capture the relevant anharmonic atomic and lattice dynamics.
Machine-learned interatomic potentials can incorporate explicit oxygen-related defect scattering in this alloy.
Quantum impurity-scattering effects dominate electronic conductivity in oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr over 0–200 K.
Activated phonon and defect scattering prevail in oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr over 300–1200 K.
Oxygen-induced point defects and local lattice distortions alter vibrational dynamics and scattering potentials in HfNbTaTiZr.
At 0–200 K, oxygen-induced defect scattering lowers conductivity non-monotonically relative to an ideal crystal.
At 300–1200 K, anharmonic lattice dynamics and activated defect scattering dominate the conductivity response.
The presence of oxygen enhances phonon scattering at high temperature.
Conventional perfect-crystal models fail to capture the oxygen-related and anharmonic scattering mechanisms.
The hybrid approach will predict lower conductivity than traditional perfect-crystal models because it represents additional scattering events.
The hybrid conductivity curves will agree more closely with experiment in both stated temperature regimes.
Defect-free analytical models typically underestimate low-temperature impurity scattering and high-temperature phonon and defect scattering in oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed applicability is limited to oxygen levels near 1 wt.% and the temperature windows 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Uncertainty in defect-potential and anharmonic-response parameterization prevents specifying an exact accuracy improvement.
The hypothesis is falsified if the hybrid model is not more than 15% closer to measured conductivity than conventional models, or if measurements remain within the conventional models' error margins.
